prohibited_recommendations: Do not diagnose MS based on non-specific white-matter lesions alone without meeting the 2024 revised McDonald criteria and excluding mimics
Do not start teriflunomide in a woman of child-bearing potential without effective contraception (teratogenic, long elimination half-life)
Do not use chronic oral corticosteroids as maintenance treatment for MS: they do not prevent relapses or disability and cause cumulative harm
Do not administer live-attenuated vaccines after initiation of B-cell depleting therapy (ocrelizumab, ofatumumab) or S1P modulators (fingolimod, ozanimod)
Do not omit spinal cord MRI in a patient with myelopathic signs even if the brain MRI alone meets DIS: cord lesions count toward DIS and separate MS from NMOSD
Do not treat a urinary infection with a cephalosporin (documented cephalosporin allergy with hives)
required_recommendations: State relapsing-remitting MS by the 2024 McDonald criteria, naming the regions that give DIS and, where needed, what gives DIT or positive CSF (here periventricular, juxtacortical, infratentorial and spinal cord, with the left optic nerve a fifth region by VEP or OCT; four or more regions need no separate DIT).

Treat the current relapse, which still limits walking, with methylprednisolone (IV 1 g daily for 3-5 days as an inpatient, or oral 500 mg daily for 5 days), after a urine dipstick and culture exclude a urinary infection given the new urgency; consider plasma exchange if a severe relapse does not respond.

Offer disease-modifying therapy after diagnosis, choosing efficacy by disease activity (three attacks in 14 months, enhancing brain and cord lesions), after discussing pregnancy plans and contraception.

Before starting disease-modifying therapy, check HBsAg, anti-HBc, HCV and VZV IgG (HIV already non-reactive), a lymphocyte count and liver function, and give any live vaccine at least 4-6 weeks before starting.

Measure the post-void residual volume; if it is low, offer an antimuscarinic (or mirabegron) for the urgency, mindful of the additive anticholinergic effect of dicyclomine; if it is raised, teach intermittent self-catheterisation.
Explain that transient worsening after hot showers (Uhthoff phenomenon) is heat-related conduction block, not a new relapse.

clinical_pearls: Uhthoff phenomenon (heat-induced transient worsening) is characteristic of demyelinating disease and should prompt MS evaluation
Lhermitte sign (electric sensation with neck flexion) localizes to the cervical spinal cord and is highly associated with MS
Open ring enhancement on MRI has high specificity for demyelinating lesions versus tumor or infection — the opening faces the cortex (gray matter)

Under the 2024 McDonald criteria, lesions in four or five regions establish MS without a test of dissemination in time; with two or three regions, dissemination in time, CSF-restricted oligoclonal bands or a raised kFLC index, or the central vein sign complete the criteria
Short-segment spinal cord lesions (<2 vertebral segments) favor MS, while longitudinally extensive lesions (>=3 segments) should raise concern for NMOSD

patient.history_present_illness: Ms. Sarah Kowalski is a 33-year-old right-handed Caucasian woman who presents to the neurology inpatient service after being referred urgently by her primary care physician for progressive left leg weakness and new-onset urinary symptoms. She reports that approximately six weeks ago, she began noticing that her left leg felt 'heavy' while climbing the stairs to her apartment, initially attributing it to fatigue from work stress. Over the following two weeks, the heaviness progressed and she noticed her left foot occasionally dragging, particularly toward the end of the day. Three weeks ago, she began experiencing urinary urgency with several episodes of near-incontinence, which she found distressing and unlike anything she had experienced before. She also reports a band-like tightness sensation around her lower abdomen that she describes as feeling like she is wearing a tight belt. On further questioning, she recalls an episode approximately eight months ago in which she developed blurred vision in her left eye lasting about ten days, accompanied by pain with eye movement. She saw her optometrist at the time, who found reduced vision in the left eye and referred her to ophthalmology, but she did not follow up on the referral as the symptoms had largely resolved. She also recalls a two-week episode of tingling in her right hand and forearm approximately fourteen months ago that resolved spontaneously and which she attributed to carpal tunnel syndrome from typing at work. She denies any recent fevers, weight loss, joint pains, oral ulcers, or skin rashes. She notes that her symptoms seem to worsen noticeably after taking hot showers, with her leg weakness becoming more pronounced for 30 to 60 minutes afterward. Over the past week, her partner has noticed that she appears more fatigued than usual and has been stumbling when walking around the apartment.
